{"id": "19:3/q20", "question": "How should wording with multiple senses be interpreted?", "turns_on": "The plain, legal and customary senses have different priorities; equal conflicting senses require indicators.", "positions": [{"id": "19:3/q20/p1", "position": "A unique sense is clear; otherwise retain the plain sense unless evidence displaces it.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says unambiguous wording reveals God's intent. Another class bears two or more senses; a hidden sense requires evidence against the plain one."}, {"id": "19:3/q20/p2", "position": "Legal usage outranks linguistic and customary usage; custom outranks linguistic usage.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī grounds legal priority in transfer and binding force, customary priority in familiar usage."}, {"id": "19:3/q20/p3", "position": "When equal senses conflict, jurists use indicators to infer intent.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī uses qurūʾ, purity or menstruation, as an incompatible pair. Each mujtahid's indicator-based conclusion is God's intended meaning for that jurist, even if another differs."}]}
{"id": "19:3/q21", "question": "What makes a distant simile effective?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:3/q21/p1", "position": "A hidden likeness appears when the relevant feature is selected from unlike objects.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī says difference and discovery delight. Ibn al-Muʿtazz likens lightning's motion to a Quran reader's opening and closing, ignoring other traits. Jarīr first pities ʿAdī's bird-and-needle image, then envies the completed pen drawing ink image. Al-Khalīl's miserly hand is another example."}]}
{"id": "19:3/q22", "question": "May ذات express God's essence?", "turns_on": "The phrase fī dhāt Allāh is read as either essence or religious cause.", "positions": [{"id": "19:3/q22/p1", "position": "No; nafs names reality directly, while ذات in the cited report concerns God's religion or law.", "reasons": "Al-Suhaylī relates nafs to nafāsa and nafīs. He rejects essence as the sense of the Abraham report's fī dhāt Allāh."}, {"id": "19:3/q22/p2", "position": "Yes; ذات can be equated with nafs, essence and existence.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān reports this as most people's view, citing the Abraham report."}]}
{"id": "19:3/q23", "question": "What evidence is given for Quranic inimitability?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:3/q23/p1", "position": "Opponents used war and accusations rather than produce a rival sūra, showing inability.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān says imitation would have been easier than war, captivity and lost property. Ibn ʿAbbās reports al-Walīd praising the Quran's sweetness, splendor, fruitfulness and force before Abū Jahl pressed him to call it transmitted sorcery. Al-Jāḥiẓ says the challenge came at the Arabs' peak in poetry, oratory, language and numbers."}]}
{"id": "19:3/q24", "question": "What does ḥaḍara mean in Arabic?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:3/q24/p1", "position": "Being present or existing, the opposite of absence, without necessarily coming to a place.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī gives this distinction."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q01", "question": "Who delivered the announcement to Zachariah?", "turns_on": "Whether direct divine speech, the angelic report of 3:39, or both are intended.", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q01/p1", "position": "God addressed Zachariah directly.", "reasons": "Al-Razi cites the surrounding direct address and says 'your Lord has said' can be God's own speech; the majority take this view. Ibn Ashur introduces the words as God's speech."}, {"id": "19:7/q01/p2", "position": "An angel or angels delivered God's announcement.", "reasons": "Muqatil names Gabriel during prayer. Al-Razi and others cite 3:39 and 'your Lord has said'; Bursevi reads the opening as angelic speech; Alusi says an angel conveys divine wording, comparing 39:53."}, {"id": "19:7/q01/p3", "position": "Both God and the angels may have announced it.", "reasons": "Al-Razi reconciles Maryam's apparent divine call with the explicit angelic announcement in 3:39 by allowing both."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q02", "question": "How does this announcement follow Zachariah's prayer?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q02/p1", "position": "An unspoken clause supplies God's answer to the prayer, fulfilled by the promise of a son.", "reasons": "Majaz supplies 'so We said'; Jishumi an answer and call; Ibn Kathir compares 3:38–39, Tabatabai 21:90, and Kuranyolu 21:90. Alusi says the promise itself counts as a prompt answer despite any delay. Mawardi and Qurtubi find honor in the answer, son, and God's naming."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q03", "question": "When did the announcement and birth occur after the prayer?", "turns_on": "Reports differ on the interval between prayer, announcement, and birth.", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q03/p1", "position": "The call came promptly and the birth within months.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan reports an immediate call; Alusi calls birth within months the common account."}, {"id": "19:7/q03/p2", "position": "The child came forty years later.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi relay this alternative delay."}, {"id": "19:7/q03/p3", "position": "The child came sixty years later.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi relay this second alternative delay."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q04", "question": "How is 'O Zachariah' read and construed?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in hamza treatment and connection to the following word.", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q04/p1", "position": "The name has an extended form Zakariyyāʾ, a final-yāʾ-sukūn form Zakariyyā, and a shortened Zakrā form.", "reasons": "Majaz compares the shortened form with Bukhtā. One recitation softens the first hamza and realizes the second; Abu Amr follows that pattern. Other Arabs reverse the treatment, according to speakers heard by Sibawayh."}, {"id": "19:7/q04/p2", "position": "Adding a hamza supplies case inflection and continuity with 'innā'.", "reasons": "Qiraat-ER also records a form with a marked pause or phonological break before 'innā'."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q05", "question": "How is 'nubašširuka' read, and what does its form convey?", "turns_on": "Form I versus doubled Form II and the rhetorical force of intensification.", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q05/p1", "position": "The doubled Form II reading intensifies the glad tidings.", "reasons": "Most readers use the doubled sh, according to Ibn Atiyya and the Nashr; Biqai says it suits news extraordinary enough to be denied. Nashr lists its occurrence alongside other loci."}, {"id": "19:7/q05/p2", "position": "The lighter Form I reading gives the same announcement without intensification.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya associates it with Ibn Masud's readers, with still b and damma on sh; Ibn Jawzi and Nasafi name Hamza. Nashr names Hamza and al-Kisai for the relevant occurrences; Qiraat-ER describes the Form I substitution. Nashr also notes a separate five-locus Prophet-address dispute and the Maryam exception for Hamza, al-Kisai, Khalaf, and Hafs."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q06", "question": "Who is the promised 'ghulām' and what does the word denote?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q06/p1", "position": "It is a male child, Yahya son of Zachariah.", "reasons": "Baghawi, Abu Hayyan, and Alusi gloss ghulam as male child; Abu Hayyan and Alusi note feminine ghulama also exists. Damghani identifies the boy, and Jishumi says he will be born to Zachariah."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q07", "question": "How does 'his name is Yahya' function grammatically and as speech?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q07/p1", "position": "'Yahya' is the predicate of 'his name'; the nominal clause describes the boy.", "reasons": "Nahhas gives the predicate analysis; Tabrisi and Samin say 'ismuhu Yahya' modifies ghulam. Damghani notes ism can denote the act of naming. Ibn Ashur sees the report as an implicit command to give this name."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q08", "question": "What is the linguistic origin and form of the name Yahya?", "turns_on": "Whether the proper name is borrowed or transferred from an Arabic present-tense verb.", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q08/p1", "position": "It is probably a foreign proper name without Arabic derivation.", "reasons": "Baydawi and Samin prefer this; Samin says properness and foreignness make it diptote. Abu Hayyan calls it apparently non-Arabic; Alusi considers this strongest because Arabs did not usually name children with Arabic words. Razi warns that proper names need only identify."}, {"id": "19:7/q08/p2", "position": "If Arabic, it is a verb transferred into a proper name.", "reasons": "Nahhas says its origin as an imperfect verb explains indeclinability and yāʾ spelling distinguishes it from the verb. Kashshaf, Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, and Samin compare Yaʿmar, Yaʿīsh, Yaʿmal, and Yamut. Alusi says Arabic and foreign analyses have different meters and diminutives."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q09", "question": "Why was the boy called Yahya?", "turns_on": "Which aspect of life, if any, the proper name is taken to describe.", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q09/p1", "position": "God gave him spiritual life through faith, obedience, knowledge, and wisdom.", "reasons": "Qatada speaks of faith or prophethood and faith; Zajjaj and Wahidi speak of knowledge and wisdom. Razi invokes 6:122 and 8:24; Jishumi adds 8:24 and 3:169 for the obedient as living. Qushayri mentions the household's worship and prophecy. Asad says he is spiritually alive and remembered."}, {"id": "19:7/q09/p2", "position": "His birth brought life to a barren womb or came from aged and infertile parents.", "reasons": "Muqatil names the aged father and barren mother; Ibn Khalawayh says both past ninety and despairing. Qushayri extends revival to lineage and memory. Qurtubi objects that the mother was barren, not merely old. Razi reports Ibn Abbas via Thalabi. Baydawi and Abu Hayyan mention the revived womb."}, {"id": "19:7/q09/p3", "position": "Religion or other people came alive through his mission.", "reasons": "Jishumi says faith would live through him a

{"id": "19:7/q10", "question": "What honor or lesson lies in God naming Yahya before birth?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q10/p1", "position": "God's choice of his name before birth specially honors Yahya and Zachariah.", "reasons": "Mawardi counts the name with answered prayer and son as divine election; Wahidi says parents usually name children. Tabatabai compares Jesus at 3:45; Asad calls it a divine promise. Biqai says the name was reserved; Bursevi's inward source adds the direct call by name."}, {"id": "19:7/q10/p2", "position": "Distinctive, refined names deserve preference.", "reasons": "Kashshaf cites a poem praising striking names and red robes and Ru'ba's answer to al-Bakri about his lineage. Qurtubi says such names are memorable and avoid mocking nicknames. Abu Hayyan adds Ru'ba's verse and al-Salt ibn Ata's account of advancing among the Barmakids. Ibn Ashur says the novel name distinguishes the child and becomes a model."}, {"id": "19:7/q10/p3", "position": "A name can be newly assigned without prior convention.", "reasons": "Jishumi infers this from the unprecedented name."}, {"id": "19:7/q10/p4", "position": "Naming before birth is possible for several figures.", "reasons": "Amr ibn Murrah lists Muhammad/Ahmad, Yahya, Jesus, Isaac, and Jacob, citing 61:6, 3:45, and 11:71. Bursevi's inward source says God inspires each person's name before creation and cites Jesus's announcement of Ahmad."}, {"id": "19:7/q10/p5", "position": "Naming Yahya before he existed shows the nonexistent can be known.", "reasons": "Jishumi draws this theological inference from the prior announcement."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q11", "question": "What does 'no samiyyan before him' mean?", "turns_on": "Whether samiyy is the literal bearer of the same name, a counterpart, a child, or a distinction in naming; counterpart claims also turn on whether special merit implies overall prophetic rank.", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q11/p1", "position": "No one before him had borne the name Yahya.", "reasons": "Qatada, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Zayd, al-Suddi and many others give the literal namesake reading; Ibn Jarir, Razi, and commentators reported by Kuranyolu prefer it. Tabari derives samiyy from being named; Razi says 19:65 needs the figurative peer sense because of its worship context but this verse does not. Some say no prior prophet bore it; Nahhas says nobody had been instructed to give it. A report has the Prophet name a later child Yahya."}, {"id": "19:7/q11/p2", "position": "No one before him was his equal or likeness.", "reasons": "Mujahid, Said ibn Jubayr, Ata, and others compare 19:65; some derive the sense from elevation or matching. Proposed singular traits include never sinning or intending sin, leadership, continence, childhood wisdom (19:12), miraculous parentage, announcing Jesus, and his novel name. Ibn Ashur says no earlier prophet combined them and prefers this reading. Razi, Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi and Kuranyolu object to any implication that Yahya outranks Abraham, Moses, or earlier prophets; Ibn Ashur answers that a special merit does not establish overall rank. Qushayri speaks of total virtues or sinlessness before and after prophethood. Bint al-Shati notes the Arabic counterpart sense."}, {"id": "19:7/q11/p3", "position": "No barren woman before had borne a child like Yahya.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas reports this exceptional parentage; Ibn Kathir stresses that Zachariah had no children and his wife was barren from youth, unlike Abraham and Sarah, citing 15:54 and 11:72–73. Some place the birth among Yahya's incomparable merits."}, {"id": "19:7/q11/p4", "position": "Zachariah had no son before Yahya.", "reasons": "Mujahid is cited for this by Mawardi. Ibn Khalawayh says the phrase can mean no child previously born to his parents; a later Ibn Abbas report pairs no prior son with the unused name and reads 19:65's samiyy as child. Bint al-Shati says she finds no such son sense in either Maryam verse."}, {"id": "19:7/q11/p5", "position": "His unique namesake status is that God named him before he existed.", "reasons": "Razi contrasts divine naming before birth with usual human naming after birth; StudyQuran relays the same explanation."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q12", "question": "Why does the verse specify 'before'?", "turns_on": "Whether the temporal limit anticipates someone later or only restricts an earlier comparison.", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q12/p1", "position": "A greater figure, Muhammad, would be created afterward.", "reasons": "Thalabi and Qurtubi relay this explanation; Jishumi agrees Muhammad came later and was superior."}, {"id": "19:7/q12/p2", "position": "It limits the claim to earlier namesakes or earlier matching qualities, without ranking every prophet.", "reasons": "Thalabi says only some qualities may be meant because earlier patriarchs were greater; Baghawi names Abraham and Moses. Jishumi says a name reading poses no rank issue. Ibn Ashur says special merit does not entail overall superiority."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q13", "question": "How are 'lam najʿal ... samiyyan' and samiyy formed grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q13/p1", "position": "'Samiyyan' is the direct object and the clause describes the boy.", "reasons": "Jishumi identifies the object; Samin says the whole clause is a genitive adjective of ghulam. Samin derives samiyy on the pattern of radiyy from sumuww, supporting the Basran origin of ism; a derivation from wasm would yield wasim."}, {"id": "19:7/q13/p2", "position": "The negative 'lam najʿal' belongs to a Qur'anic rhetorical pattern about what God did not make.", "reasons": "Zarkashi compares ma jaʿala clauses and says these patterns signal whether renewal of the named matter is expected."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q14", "question": "What reports describe Yahya's freedom from sin?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q14/p1", "position": "Yahya alone neither committed nor even intended sin.", "reasons": "Sulami quotes the Prophet without a grade; Razi reports it through Ikrima from Ibn Abbas, and Alusi says such reports are numerous. These reports support his claimed lack of a peer."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q15", "question": "What reports connect Yahya with Husayn?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q15/p1", "position": "Husayn likewise had an unprecedented name and shared a martyr's fate.", "reasons": "Tabrisi reports Abu Abd Allah's saying that the sky reddened morning and evening for forty mornings and the killers of both men were illegitimate; StudyQuran describes the Shiite tradition of Husayn's name given by the Prophet and martyrdom under Yazid. Ali Zayn al-Abidin says Husayn recalled at every stop that Yahya's head was presented to an adulteress."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q16", "question": "What does the Gospel account report about John's announcement and naming?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q16/p1", "position": "Gabriel announced John to the elderly, righteous priest Zechariah and Elizabeth; after birth both parents affirmed the name John.", "reasons": "Tabatabai reports the Gospel: Elizabeth is Aaronite and childless; the child will avoid wine, receive the Spirit, and prepare Israel in Elijah's spirit. Relatives object to the name, Zechariah writes it, regains speech, praises God and prophesies."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q17", "question": "How does the Qur'an's account of Zachariah and Mary lead to this promise?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q17/p1", "position": "Zachariah's care of Mary and the provision he saw with her prompted his prayer for a righteous child despite barrenness.", "reasons": "Tabatabai cites 3:37–41 and 6:85, 6:87: Zachariah is a prophet and guardian of Mary after Imran's death. A report specifies out-of-season fruit. Tabatabai says even if accepted, the fruit explains hope, and inheritance cannot mean nonhereditary spiritual stations without evidence. Angels announced John during prayer and a three-day inability to speak became a sign."}, {"id": "19:7/q17/p2", "position": "The two birth stories display divine creative power beyond ordinary bodily limits.", "reasons": "StudyQuran connects Mary, Zachariah, John and Jesus with 3:35, 3:62, 21:89, and 21:91."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q18", "question": "What lesson does the answered prayer teach about supplication?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q18/p1", "position": "Sincere need and prayer can be answered despite apparently hopeless circumstances.", "reasons": "Bursevi says God opens prayer as a sign mercy opens, wholly or partly; a report s

Razi says Zachariah's request served religion."}, {"id": "19:7/q18/p3", "position": "A supplicant should address God as 'My Lord'.", "reasons": "Razi draws this practice from Zachariah's address."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q19", "question": "How does John's birth fit the sura's argument about Jesus?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q19/p1", "position": "John's birth to an old man and barren woman introduces Mary's story and refutes the inference that Jesus's miraculous birth makes him divine.", "reasons": "Islahi says John neither claimed divinity nor was made a god; the sura also presents prophets' monotheism, prayer, and zakah against later followers' innovations, counsels Muhammad to persevere against opponents mistaking respite for vindication, and addresses the People of the Book amid their support of Quraysh. Abu Hayyan links this sura's wondrous births with the previous sura's Cave, Moses-Khidr and Dhu al-Qarnayn stories."}, {"id": "19:7/q19/p2", "position": "The parallel in Al Imran gives a fuller announcement and correspondingly fuller gratitude and sign.", "reasons": "Samarrai says 3:39 has more attributes; 3:41 specifies three days, with clearer daytime remembrance, versus Maryam's three nights at 19:10. {"id": "19:7/q20", "question": "What inward meanings are drawn from the promised boy and his name?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q20/p1", "position": "The boy is the heart, born of spirit and soul, and Yahya names its enduring spiritual life.", "reasons": "Qashani says Zachariah seeks a sign to reach this heart; it receives wisdom and the book of discriminating intellect. Silence avoids sensory concerns; faculties continue disciplined worship. Divine tenderness, purity and piety signify attribute manifestation, detachment and avoidance of soul traits; peace, birth, death and resurrection signify release from material entanglement, manifestation, annihilation and life in God."}, {"id": "19:7/q20/p2", "position": "The written shape and symmetry of Yahya's name symbolize divine enabling, tenderness, verification and sinlessness.", "reasons": "Al-Subayh reads its two yāʾs around the ḥāʾ and says the name reads in either direction. Junayd says obedience keeps Yahya praiseworthy and without blame."}, {"id": "19:7/q20/p3", "position": "God's personal address, prior naming and singular name are inward honors.", "reasons": "Bursevi's Najmi reading says John never desired or intended sin."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q21", "question": "What other literary or scholarly observations are made about the verse?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q21/p1", "position": "The verse exemplifies rare Qur'anic vocabulary and the rhetorical design of divine non-making clauses.", "reasons": "Zarkashi lists these phrases in works on gharib al-Qur'an and says Qur'anic styles disclose the inimitable composition, arrangement, sweetness and fluency."}, {"id": "19:7/q21/p2", "position": "The sura's opening letters can symbolically summarize its figures.", "reasons": "Elmalili tentatively maps Kāf to Zachariah, Hā to his wife, Yā to John, ʿAyn to Jesus, and Ṣād to Mustafa."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q22", "question": "Where was this sura revealed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q22/p1", "position": "The sura is Meccan, with a reported exception for its prostration verse.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan says Muqatil places that verse in Medina after the migration to Abyssinia."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q23", "question": "What additional report compares Ahmad's name with the other prenatally announced names?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q23/p1", "position": "Ahmad in Jesus's prophecy indicates Muhammad is more praiseworthy than Jesus and predecessors.", "reasons": "Al-Raghib is cited on 61:6 in the context of names announced before birth."}]}
{"id": "19:7/q24", "question": "What does the report say of Gabriel announcing Yahya and his name?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "19:7/q24/p1", "position": "Gabriel announced Yahya, whose name is linked to living and counted among God's names.", "reasons": "The Ibn Abbas report gives these details."}]}
{"id": "19:42/q01", "question": "How is 'when he said' attached to the preceding description of Abraham?", "turns_on": "Whether idh is appositional or governed by kāna or the preceding descriptions, and whether those parses meet the grammatical objections.", "positions": [{"id": "19:42/q01/p1", "position": "It is an appositive of inclusion to Abraham.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn cites an earlier parallel at 19:16 and notes the intervening 'he was truthful, a prophet'; Bursawī and Ibn ʿĀshūr take the time as specifying Abraham, and Ibn ʿĀshūr says this moment merits remembrance. Al-Ālūsī acknowledges objections about an uncoordinated substitute and the usual indeclinability of idh, yet prefers this parse."}, {"id": "19:42/q01/p2", "position": "It depends on kāna, with the description intervening parenthetically.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī allows the parenthesis; al-Nasafī reports the attachment. The Shaykh objects that governing a temporal adverb by kāna is disputed; al-Ālūsī notes further grammatical problems."}, {"id": "19:42/q01/p3", "position": "It depends on ṣiddīqan nabiyyan or its descriptive sense: Abraham had both qualities when he spoke.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, Abū al-Baqāʾ, al-Nasafī and al-Samīn give the reading. The Shaykh objects that a compound cannot jointly govern the adverb, ṣiddīq is already modified unless Kufan grammar is used, and dependence on nabī would imply prophethood began then."}]}
{"id": "19:42/q02", "question": "Who was the father Abraham addressed?", "turns_on": "Whether ab denotes a biological father here or a figurative paternal relative; sources appeal to the plain Qur'anic wording, other family passages, and reported identifications.", "positions": [{"id": "19:42/q02/p1", "position": "He was Āzar, Abraham's father.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿĀshūr name Āzar; al-Jishumī calls him an unbeliever and cites other Qur'anic verses against figurative reinterpretation. Al-Ḍamghānī and Ibn al-Jawzī cite this as an instance of ab meaning an actual father, with 6:74 and other family passages.
